Monday.grammar: Acronyms: first letters make a word

Thursday.grammar: Acronyms: which one does your reader need?

extra_task.prompt: Give me one word built from chron, meaning time.
Give me one word built from eco, meaning house.
Give me one word built from pend or pens, meaning hang or pay.

words_to_read_review.notes:
1. READ: "Okay, if you were born in January, February or March, read row 1."
2. READ: "If you were born in April, May or June, read row 2."
3. READ: "If you were born in July, August or September, read row 3."
4. READ: "If you were born in October, November or December, read row 4."
5. READ: "Everyone reads row 5." Every student reads at least two rows in the group round.
6. ASK: "pend and pens mean hang or pay. Which four words carry them?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: pendulum, dispense, appendix, suspense.
7. ASK: "pon and pound mean place or part. Which four words carry them?" 5 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: exponent, postpone, ponderous, proponent.
8. ASK: "jur, jud and just mean right or law. Which two words carry them?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: adjudicate, injurious.
9. ASK: "Which word names an animal that eats insects?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: insectivore.
10. ASK: "chron means time. Which word means to make two things run at the same time?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: synchronise.
11. ASK: "Which word means to put something off until later?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: postpone.
12. ASK: "Make juncture plural." 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: junctures.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our canteen expenditure on hot food climbs every winter.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pend and pens mean hang or pay. Which of those two is working here?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The paying one. Ex means out, so expenditure is the money paid out.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The council will impound any bike left on the tram tracks.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pound means place. Where does an impounded bike get placed?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Into a locked council yard. Im means in, so it goes in and stays there.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The netball club had to compensate the school for the broken gate.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pens means pay. Who ends up with the money here?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The school. Com means together, so both sides finish level again.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our opponent in the grand final has not lost a game all year.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pon means place. Where is an opponent placed?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Straight across from you. Op means against, so they are placed against your team.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The koala showed real independence within a week of leaving its mother.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pend means hang. Which taught ending turns not hanging into a state?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ence ending, the same one in existence. Independence is the state of not hanging on anyone.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our dog has a propensity for stealing socks off the line.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pens means hang. Which taught ending turns it into a quality you carry?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ity ending, the same one in gravity. A propensity is a leaning that hangs on you.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The librarian wrote a recommendation for our next class novel.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: mend means entrust. What is the librarian entrusting you with?
words_to_spell_review.answer: A judgement about the book, handed over so you can trust the choice without reading it first.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Speeding on that highway sits in the state police jurisdiction.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: jur means law. What does a jurisdiction fence off?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The area where that law can be used. Step outside it and those police have no power.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The ship's chronometer kept perfect time right across the Pacific.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: chron means time. Why did a ship need one of these?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Exact time told sailors how far east or west they had travelled. No chronometer meant no position.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: A bin chicken is omnivorous, so almost anything counts as food.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: vore means eating. Which taught part tells you it eats everything?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The omni part, meaning all. Omni plus vore is eating all, so nothing is off the menu.

words_to_read_new.meaning: caus is the root on its own, cause: the thing that makes something else happen
be means by + cause: by the cause of it
ex means out + cuse means cause: the cause that gets you out of trouble
ac means toward + cuse means cause: to point the cause toward a person
caus means cause + al means relating to: relating to what made it happen
ac means toward + cus means cause + er means the person: the person who points the cause at you
ac means toward + cus means cause + ed means already done: the person the cause has been pointed at
ex means out + cus means cause + ed means already done: let out of it, the cause accepted
ex means out + cus means cause + able means able to be: able to be let off
caus means cause + ing means happening now: making it happen right now
caus means cause + ation means the act of: the act of one thing making another happen
ac means toward + cus means cause + ory means relating to: relating to pointing the cause at someone

associated_word_exceptions.reason: ground 3 - simpler and more transparent than causality, and it is the base students need before causality makes sense
ground 1 - the captured card lists only ten words; accused is the everyday form students meet in news reports
ground 1 - the captured card lists only ten words; excused is the school form students meet on absence notes
ground 1 - the captured card lists only ten words; causing keeps the root visible in its commonest verb form

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Okay, learn caus and cus once and a whole family of blame and reason words opens up - and you will finally see why because ends the way it does."
READ each word as it appears, then connect caus or cus to the card meaning: cause.
cause - caus is the root on its own, cause: the thing that makes something else happen.
because - be means by + cause: by the cause of it. That is why because answers the question why.
excuse - ex means out + cuse means cause: the cause you offer to get out of trouble.
accuse - ac means toward + cuse means cause: to point the cause toward a person.
causal - caus means cause + al means relating to: relating to what made it happen.
accuser - ac means toward + cus means cause + er means the person: the person who points the cause at you.
accused - ac means toward + cus means cause + ed means already done: the person the cause has been pointed at.
excused - ex means out + cus means cause + ed means already done: let out of it, because the cause was accepted.
excusable - ex means out + cus means cause + able means able to be: able to be let off.
causing - caus means cause + ing means happening now: making it happen right now.
causation - caus means cause + ation means the act of: the act of one thing making another happen.
accusatory - ac means toward + cus means cause + ory means relating to: relating to pointing the cause at somebody. A blaming voice.
Memory hook: picture the courtroom finger. accuse points the cause AT a person, excuse pushes the cause AWAY. Ask of any caus word: who is being blamed? Challenge: catch three caus words in one news story this week.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "Okay, when you finish, write one sentence that uses cause and because and shows what caused what."
2. CHECK: the sentence must show the cause doing the causing, not just use the word.
EXTENSION: Build the longest real caus or cus word you can, then write its morpheme sum.
Name every part you can, and put a question mark on any part you have not been taught yet.
Answer: e.g. inexcusable = in (not) + ex (out) + cus (cause) + able (able to be).

new_morph_activity.title: Meaning sums for caus and cus
new_morph_activity.rule: caus and cus mean cause. Write the real word for each meaning.
new_morph_activity.example:
One done for you:
the cause pointed at a person = accuse
Word bank: cause  because  excuse  causal
items: 1. the thing that makes it happen = ?    2. by the cause of = ?
3. the cause you give to get out = ?    4. relating to a cause = ?
new_morph_activity.footer: Check: can you hear cause in your word?
new_morph_activity.notes:
ANSWER: 1 cause, 2 because, 3 excuse, 4 causal.
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one first. The cause pointed at a person is accuse."
2. SAY: "Now pick the right word from the bank for each meaning. Three minutes, then write it... chin it... show me."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "cause is hiding inside three of those four bank words - find it first, then read what is stuck on the front." Then do number one together.
4. SCAN all boards. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> build number two together, then re-ask.
TRAP: writing cause for number two. Fix: say number two has an extra part at the front meaning by, student rewrites because.
EXTENSION: Write causal as its parts, then build one more caus word that names a person.
HELP: Cover two bank words at a time so each meaning has only two choices left.
---
Purpose: day one turns the card meaning cause into four real words students already say. [You Do | Meaning sums | Morphology]
ANSWERS:
1. the thing that makes it happen = cause
2. by the cause of = because
3. the cause you give to get out = excuse
4. relating to a cause = causal
EXTENSION: causal splits into caus and al. One more: accuser, the person who points the cause at you.
new_morph_activity.check_title: Tick it or fix it - meaning sums for caus
new_morph_activity.check_rule: Tick each correct word. Fix any word that does not match.
check_items: 1. cause = the caus root on its own: what makes it happen
2. because = be (by) + cause: by the cause of it
3. excuse = ex (out) + cus (cause): gets you out of it
4. causal = caus (cause) + al (relating to): about the cause
new_morph_activity.check_footer: Every answer hides caus or cus
new_morph_activity.check_notes:
ANSWER: 1 cause, 2 because, 3 excuse, 4 causal.
1. MODEL: "Number two says by the cause of. Cause is the whole root, and be means by, so the word has to be because."
2. SAY: "Now tick each word that matches. Fix any word that is different."
3. ASK: "Which one of these four words is not about blame at all?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: cause.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> rebuild number three together, then re-check.
TRAP: ticking a word that is spelled wrong. Fix: read the green word chunk by chunk, then rewrite it.
EXTENSION: Predict what accusation will mean before we meet it tomorrow.
HELP: Find caus or cus inside the green word first, then read the part in front of it.
---
Purpose: protected reveal so every student hears how each caus word is built. [You Do | Feedback | Morphology]

review.notes:
Why learned: the l is silent, exactly like salmon, and the o says a long /oh/.
Say it: YOHK, one beat. Write y - ol - k, then check the l is still sitting there.
Quick link: the yolk feeds a growing chick, so it belongs in every life cycle diagram.

Why learned: the l is completely silent, so the word sounds like sam-on but keeps a letter you never hear.
Say it: SAM-uhn, two beats. Write sal - mon in two chunks and leave the l in.
Quick link: salmon swim upriver to spawn, so the word belongs in every food chain and river unit.

new.notes:
Why learned: the th sits in the middle of the word and says nothing at all, so you write two letters you never hear.
Say it: AST-muh, two beats. Write as - th - ma in three chunks and leave the th in the middle.
Link: asthma turns up in every health and PE unit, and on the sport permission notes you take home.
You will write this word on your own health form and in your PE reflections this term.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Name an acronym, and use brackets so a reader is never stuck on letters they cannot unpack.
WHY THIS WEEK: students write ANZAC, GPS and CFA in their reports and never tell the reader what the letters stand for.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards and no scoring - books, thumbs and voices only.
PREP: an acronym is a short word built from the first letters of a longer name. Round brackets are the tool that expands it.

i_do.title: First letters make a word
i_do.rule: An acronym is a short word made from the first letters of a longer name.
i_do.example:
Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
ANZAC
items: Take the first letter of each important word.
Say the short one as a word, not letter by letter.
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: what do the letters stand for?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: ANZAC is built from the first letter of Australian, New, Zealand, Army and Corps.
1. SAY: "Okay, your reports are full of short forms like this one. If your reader cannot unpack one, they stop. Watch where this one comes from."
2. WRITE: copy "Australian and New Zealand Army Corps" onto the class board. POINT at Australian and say that is where we start.
3. WRITE: circle the first letter of Australian, New, Zealand, Army and Corps, then write ANZAC underneath, so the class board shows both forms.
4. SAY: "Five words, five letters, one short word. That is an acronym, and we say it as a word - ANZAC, not A N Z A C."
TRAP: taking a letter from the little word and. Fix: say we only use the important words, student reads the circled letters again.
CLARIFY: if a student asks about ones we spell out, like ABC, say those are read letter by letter, and this week we treat both the same way.
---
Purpose: day one names the acronym and builds one letter by letter in front of the class. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: strictly, letter-by-letter ones are initialisms; this week treat any first-letter shortening as an acronym and focus on unpacking it.

we_do.title: Build the acronym
we_do.rule: An acronym takes the first letter of each important word.
we_do.example:
Country Fire Authority -> ?
Radio Detection And Ranging -> ?
items: Take the first letter of each important word.
Say it as a word if the letters make one.
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: CFA and RADAR.
1. SAY: "Okay, my turn is over. I give you the long name, you give me the short one."
2. ASK: "What is the acronym for Country Fire Authority?" 10 sec, everyone together on three. EXPECT: CFA.
3. ASK: "What is the acronym for Radio Detection And Ranging?" 10 sec, everyone together on three. EXPECT: RADAR. Then cold call one student to name the letter each word gave.
4. SCAN the room for voices. 80%+ -> move on. Less -> circle the first letters on the board together, then re-ask.
TRAP: reading RADAR letter by letter. Fix: say those five letters make a word we can say, student says radar out loud.
CLARIFY: if a student asks why CFA is not said as a word, say cfa is not sayable, so we spell that one out and say radar as a word.
---
Purpose: guided oral practice so every student builds an acronym before writing one. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: RADAR really is an acronym from the 1940s; most people have forgotten it was ever a full name.

you_do.title: Write the acronym
you_do.rule: Your turn: write the acronym for each name in your OG book.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
= ANZAC
items: A) Very Important Person = ?    B) As Soon As Possible = ?
C) Do It Yourself = ?    D) Personal Best = ?
you_do.footer: Check: does your short form use every big word?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A VIP, B ASAP, C DIY, D PB.
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one first. Five important words gave five letters, and they spell ANZAC."
2. SAY: "Write A, B, C and D down the page, then write the acronym beside each. Two minutes, on your own."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "cover everything except the first letter of each word and read what is left." Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> build C together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: taking a letter from as or a. Fix: say the small joining words are skipped, student rewrites B.
EXTENSION: Write one acronym said as a word and one said letter by letter, then write a rule for what decides which way a reader says it.
HELP: Give the four answers out of order; students match each answer to A, B, C or D and then say why.
---
Purpose: independent practice building acronyms from everyday names. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) Very Important Person = VIP
B) As Soon As Possible = ASAP
C) Do It Yourself = DIY
D) Personal Best = PB
EXTENSION: said as a word - ANZAC, RADAR, ASAP. Said letter by letter - VIP, DIY, PB, CFA. The rule: if the letters make a sayable pattern of consonants and vowels we say it as a word, and if they do not we spell it out.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - write the acronym
you_do.check_rule: Tick each correct acronym. Fix any that skips or adds a letter.
check_items: A) Very Important Person = VIP, three first letters
B) As Soon As Possible = ASAP, said as a word
C) Do It Yourself = DIY, three first letters
D) Personal Best = PB, two first letters
you_do.check_footer: Editing move: check your reader knows it.
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A VIP, B ASAP, C DIY, D PB.
1. MODEL: "For A I took the V from Very, the I from Important and the P from Person. Three big words, three letters, VIP."
2. SAY: "Now tick each acronym that matches. Fix any that skips or adds a letter."
3. ASK: "Which of these four can you say straight out as a word?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: ASAP.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> rebuild B together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "Next time you write a short form in a report, stop and ask whether your reader has met it before."
TRAP: writing lower case letters. Fix: say each letter came from a capital at the start of a word, student rewrites it in capitals.
---
Purpose: protected reveal that models the first-letter move and sends it into their own writing. [You Do | Feedback | Grammar | HITS 5]

extra_task.prompt: Give me one word built from carn or carni, meaning flesh or meat.
Give me one word built from junct or join, meaning join.
Give me one word built from mand or mend, meaning order or entrust.

words_to_read_review.notes:
1. READ: "Okay, if your first name starts with A to F, read row 1."
2. READ: "If it starts with G to L, read row 2."
3. READ: "If it starts with M to R, read row 3."
4. READ: "If it starts with S to Z, read row 4."
5. READ: "Everyone reads row 5." Every student reads at least two rows in the group round.
6. ASK: "pend and pens mean hang or pay. Which three words carry them?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: appendage, pendant, impend.
7. ASK: "pon and pound mean place or part. Which three words carry them?" 5 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: compound, exponential, expound.
8. ASK: "caus and cus mean cause. Which two words carry them?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: cause, excuse.
9. ASK: "mand means order. Which two words carry it?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: mandate, commander.
10. ASK: "Which word names a written record of events in time order?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: chronicle.
11. ASK: "Which word means found guilty in court?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: convicted.
12. ASK: "Which word names a picture that stands for a word or an idea?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: pictograph.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: A one week suspension kept our best defender off the court.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pens means hang. What is left hanging during a suspension?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The player's place in the team. It hangs there, kept for them, until the week is up.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our coach told the whole squad that nobody here is dispensable.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which taught root is hiding in the middle of dispensable?
words_to_spell_review.answer: pens, meaning hand out. Something dispensable can be handed away and never missed.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The postponement of sports day gave us one more week of practice.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pon means place. Which taught prefix tells you where the day was moved to?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The post part, meaning after. The whole day slides back to a later date.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our teacher asked us to ponder the ending before writing anything.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pon means place. What are you placing when you ponder?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Ideas, side by side in your head, until one of them finally fits.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The principal had to countermand the note about early dismissal.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which two taught parts are stacked in countermand?
words_to_spell_review.answer: counter, meaning against, and mand, meaning order. It is an order sent against an order.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The umpire made one prejudicial remark about our whole side.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: jud means law or right. Which taught ending turns prejudice into a describing word?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -cial ending, the same one in facial. Something prejudicial tips a decision before the facts arrive.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our netball team looked invincible until the final quarter.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: vinc means conquer. What has to be true for a team to be invincible?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Nobody can beat them at all. In means not, so they cannot be conquered.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The word although works as a conjunction in that sentence.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: junct means join. What is a conjunction holding together?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Two parts of one sentence. Con means together, so it keeps them side by side.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: We stayed inside at lunch because the storm had not passed.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cause is the whole root here. Which little part sits in front of it?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The be part, meaning by. Because tells the reader by what cause something happened.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Ana was excused from swimming after handing in a note.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cus means cause. Who accepted the cause here?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The teacher. Once the note explained the cause, Ana was let out of the lesson.

words_to_read_new.meaning: caus means cause + al means relating to + -ity means the state of: the state of one thing causing another
caus means cause + -ive means relating to: relating to being the cause
ac means toward + cus means cause + ation means the act of: the act of pointing the cause at a person
in means not + ex means out + cus means cause + able means able to be: not able to be let off
un means not + ex means out + cus means cause + ed means already done: not let off, never explained
ac means toward + cus means cause + ing means happening now: pointing the cause at someone right now
ex means out + cus means cause + ing means happening now: letting the cause out, letting someone off
caus means cause + s means more than one: the things that make something happen
caus means cause + al means relating to + ly means in that way: linked the way a cause is linked to what follows

ground 1 - the captured card lists only ten words; accusation is the everyday noun students meet in news reports
ground 3 - everyday school word (an unexcused absence) built from un- plus the card word excused
ground 1 - the captured card lists only ten words; accusing keeps the root visible in its commonest verb form
ground 1 - the captured card lists only ten words; excusing pairs with accusing to show the two directions of the root

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Okay, same root as yesterday. Today we stack more parts on top of it, and the words get longer without getting harder."
READ each word as it appears, then connect caus or cus to the card meaning: cause.
causality - caus means cause + al means relating to + -ity means the state of: the state of one thing causing another.
causative - caus means cause + -ive means relating to: relating to being the cause. A causative factor is the thing that made it happen.
accusation - ac means toward + cus means cause + ation means the act of: the act of pointing the cause at a person.
inexcusable - in means not + ex means out + cus means cause + able means able to be: not able to be let off. No cause is good enough.
unexcused - un means not + ex means out + cus means cause + ed means already done: not let off, because nobody ever explained it.
accusing - ac means toward + cus means cause + ing means happening now: pointing the cause at someone right now.
excusing - ex means out + cus means cause + ing means happening now: letting the cause out, letting somebody off.
causes - caus means cause + s means more than one: the things that make something happen.
causally - caus means cause + al means relating to + ly means in that way: linked the way a cause is linked to what follows.
Memory hook: picture the courtroom finger. accuse points the cause AT a person, excuse pushes the cause AWAY. Ask of any caus word: who is being blamed? Challenge: catch three caus words in one news story this week.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "Okay, when you finish, write the same event twice - once accusing somebody, once excusing them."
2. CHECK: the two sentences must keep the same event and change only the direction of the cause.
EXTENSION: Rewrite your accusing sentence so it stays polite but still points at the cause, then write one line on what you had to change.
Answer: e.g. accusing - Sam left the gate open and the dog got out. Polite - the gate was left open, and that is how the dog got out. The change is that the cause stays and the person disappears.

new_morph_activity.title: Write the sum for each word
new_morph_activity.rule: caus and cus mean cause. Write each word as its parts.
new_morph_activity.example:
One done for you:
accuser = ac (toward) + cus (cause) + er
the person who points the cause at you
items: 1. causal    2. accusation    3. unexcused    4. causality
Write the parts, then write what the whole word means.
new_morph_activity.footer: Which word has the most parts?
new_morph_activity.notes:
ANSWER: 1 caus and al, 2 ac and cus and ation, 3 un and ex and cus and ed, 4 caus and al and -ity.
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one. Accuser breaks into three parts, and the meaning underneath is those three parts joined up."
2. SAY: "Split each word into its parts, then write what the whole word means in your own words. Four minutes in your OG books."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "find caus or cus first and put a line either side of it - whatever is left is the other parts." Then split number one together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> split number three together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: splitting unexcused into un and excused and stopping. Fix: say excused still has parts inside it, student splits it again.
EXTENSION: Write the sum for causative, then use it in a sentence that shows what it means.
HELP: Give the parts of each word out of order; students put them back in the right order first.
---
Purpose: day two makes students take the longer family words apart for themselves. [You Do | Literal meanings | Morphology]
ANSWERS:
1. causal = caus (cause) + al (relating to): about what made it happen
2. accusation = ac (toward) + cus (cause) + ation (the act of): the act of blaming
3. unexcused = un (not) + ex (out) + cus (cause) + ed: never explained, never let off
4. causality = caus (cause) + al (relating to) + -ity (the state of): the link between a cause and what follows
EXTENSION: causative = caus (cause) + -ive (relating to). Sentence: heavy rain was the causative factor in the flood.

words_to_read_new.meaning: caus is the root on its own, cause: the thing that makes something else happen
be means by + cause: by the cause of it
ex means out + cuse means cause: the cause that gets you out of trouble
ac means toward + cuse means cause: to point the cause toward a person
ac means toward + cus means cause + er means the person: the person who points the cause at you
caus means cause + al means relating to: relating to what made it happen
caus means cause + ation means the act of: the act of one thing making another happen
ac means toward + cus means cause + ory means relating to: relating to pointing the cause at someone
caus means cause + al means relating to + -ity means the state of: the state of one thing causing another

associated_word_exceptions.reason: ground 3 - simpler and more transparent than causality, and it is the base students need before causality makes sense

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Okay, third day on this root. Today watch the direction - some of these point the cause at a person, and some push it away."
READ each word as it appears, then say which way the cause is pointing.
cause - caus is the root on its own, cause: the thing that makes something else happen. No direction yet.
because - be means by + cause: by the cause of it. Any sentence with because is handing over a reason.
excuse - ex means out + cuse means cause: the cause that gets you out. Direction: away from you.
accuse - ac means toward + cuse means cause: to point the cause toward a person. Direction: at somebody.
accuser - ac means toward + cus means cause + er means the person: the person doing the pointing.
causal - caus means cause + al means relating to: relating to what made it happen. A causal link joins the cause to the result.
causation - caus means cause + ation means the act of: the act of one thing making another happen.
accusatory - ac means toward + cus means cause + ory means relating to: relating to pointing the cause at somebody. A blaming tone.
causality - caus means cause + al means relating to + -ity means the state of: the state of one thing causing another.
Memory hook: picture the courtroom finger. accuse points the cause AT a person, excuse pushes the cause AWAY. Ask of any caus word: who is being blamed? Challenge: catch three caus words in one news story this week.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "Okay, when you finish, write one sentence where a causal link is doing the work - this happened, and that is why."
2. CHECK: a reader must be able to point at the cause and at the result.
EXTENSION: Find a caus or cus word that is not on the board, write its morpheme sum with a question mark on any part you have not been taught, then write one sentence where a reader could work out the meaning.
Answer: e.g. inexcusable = in (not) + ex (out) + cus (cause) + able (able to be). Sentence: leaving the tap running all night was inexcusable, because there was no reason for it at all.

PURPOSE: Name an acronym, and use brackets so a reader is never stuck on letters they cannot unpack.

i_do.title: Brackets do the explaining
i_do.rule: Give the full name once, then the short form in round brackets.
i_do.example: The Country Fire Authority (CFA) sent two trucks.
items: Full name first, short form in the brackets.
After that, the short form on its own is enough.
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: which one does your reader need?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: the full name comes first, and the short form sits in round brackets straight after it.
1. SAY: "Okay, this is the move that stops a reader getting stuck. You explain the short form once, and then you never explain it again."
2. WRITE: copy "The CFA sent two trucks." onto the class board. POINT at CFA and say a new reader stops right here.
3. WRITE: rub out CFA and write "Country Fire Authority (CFA)" in its place, so the class board now reads the whole sentence again.
4. SAY: "Full name, then the short form in brackets. From here on in that piece of writing, CFA on its own is enough."
TRAP: putting the full name inside the brackets instead. Fix: say the brackets hold the short form, student rewrites it with CFA inside them.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether they can start with the short form, say yes - CFA (Country Fire Authority) works too, as long as one of the two is in the brackets.
---
Purpose: day three gives students the bracket move that makes a short form usable. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: the test for brackets is that the sentence still works if you cover them; here it does, because the full name is already there.

we_do.title: Put the brackets in
we_do.rule: Say where the brackets go and what belongs inside them.
we_do.example: The Australian Broadcasting Corporation ABC ran the story.
items: The short form goes inside the brackets.

we_do.notes:
ANSWER: the brackets go around ABC - the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) ran the story.
1. SAY: "Okay, this sentence has both forms in it already, but no brackets, so it reads like a stumble."
2. ASK: "Which three letters belong inside the brackets?" 10 sec, everyone together on three. EXPECT: ABC.
3. ASK: "Say the whole sentence back with the brackets in." 15 sec, everyone together on three. EXPECT: the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) ran the story.
4. SCAN the room for voices. 80%+ -> cold call one student to say why the full name goes first, then move on. Less -> read the sentence both ways, then re-ask.
TRAP: putting brackets around the full name. Fix: say cover the brackets and the sentence must still make sense, student re-reads it and moves them.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether commas would do the same job, say they can, but brackets tell the reader this is a quick aside they can skip.

9. ASK: "chron means time. Which word names something sitting in the wrong time period?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: anachronism.
10. ASK: "-ule means small. Which word names a tiny round drop?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: globule.
11. ASK: "Which word means to join two things together?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: conjoin.
12. ASK: "Which word means you won?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: victorious.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The map we needed was in the appendix at the back of the book.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pend means hang. Where does an appendix hang?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Off the end. Ap means onto, so it is added on after the real book has finished.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The pendant on that chain came from my great grandmother.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pend means hang. Which taught ending turns it into a thing?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ant ending, the same one in accountant. A pendant is simply the thing that hangs.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Salt is a compound, so two different elements are locked inside it.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pound means part. How many parts make a compound?
words_to_spell_review.answer: At least two. Com means together, so the parts are placed together and stay that way.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our class has a propensity for talking straight through the roll.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pens means hang. What does a propensity make you do without deciding to?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Lean the same way every time. It hangs on you, so it shows up before you have thought.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The new mandate says every rider wears a helmet on camp.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: mand means order. What makes a mandate different from a suggestion?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Nobody gets to opt out of it. A mandate is an order, so it applies to every single rider.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The judiciary is the part of government that runs the courts.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: jud means law. Who belongs to the judiciary?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The judges. They decide what the law means, and they are not the ones who write it.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: We had to synchronise our watches before the orienteering start.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: chron means time. Which taught prefix tells you the watches match?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The syn part, meaning together. Synchronise puts every watch on the same time at once.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: One weed can change a whole creek ecosystem in a single summer.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: eco means house. Who lives in the house here?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Every living thing in the creek. The system is how they share the one home.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Nobody could agree on the cause of the power failure.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: This is the root on its own. What is a cause always attached to?
words_to_spell_review.answer: A result. There is no cause without something that happened afterwards.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: It is unfair to accuse somebody before you have heard them.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cus means cause. Which way is the cause pointing in accuse?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Toward a person. Ac means toward, so the cause lands on somebody by name.

review.notes:
Why learned: the y does the vowel's job, and the second beat has no vowel letter at all.
Say it: RITH-uhm, two beats. Write rhy - thm, then check the h behind the r.
Quick link: every poem and every song has a rhythm, so you will write it in English and in music.

Why learned: the th in the middle says nothing at all, so two of the letters are silent passengers.
Say it: AST-muh, two beats. Write as - th - ma, then check the th is still in the middle.
Quick link: an asthma plan lives in the first aid folder, so the word is on a form you may have to read.

dictation.sentence: Our coach was judicious and gave the injured player a rest.
dictation.focus: revision from two weeks ago: jud and jur in judicious and injured

dictation.sentence: Before the storm arrived, the commander checked the ship's chronometer and marked the time.

punctuation: comma after the opening subordinate clause (the before part that cannot stand alone - the comma shows where it ends)
apostrophe for the missing letters in ship's (the chronometer belonging to the ship)

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Name an acronym, and use brackets so a reader is never stuck on letters they cannot unpack.
WHY THIS WEEK: students write ANZAC, GPS and CFA in their reports and never tell the reader what the letters stand for.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards and no scoring - books, thumbs and voices only.
PREP: today is the judgement call - brackets on the first mention, short form on its own after that.

i_do.title: Which one does your reader need?
i_do.rule: First time you use it: full name, then brackets.
i_do.example:
We rang the SES.
We rang the State Emergency Service (SES).
items: First time: full name plus brackets.
After that: the short form on its own.
i_do.footer: Check: has your reader met this one yet?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: the second version works for a new reader, because the full name is there once with the short form in brackets.
1. SAY: "Okay, last day on this. The whole week comes down to one question: has my reader met this short form yet?"
2. WRITE: copy "We rang the SES." onto the class board. POINT at SES and say a reader who has never met it stops here.
3. WRITE: underneath, write "We rang the State Emergency Service (SES)." so the class board shows the weak version above the strong one.
4. SAY: "One extra bracket and three extra words, and now anybody can read it. Later in the same piece, SES on its own is plenty."
TRAP: unpacking the same short form every single time. Fix: say once is enough in one piece of writing, student reads the second mention with SES alone.
CLARIFY: if a student asks about a short form everybody knows, say if you are unsure whether your reader knows it, unpack it - it costs three words and saves a stumble.
---
Purpose: day four turns the bracket move into a decision students make while drafting. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: the SES is the State Emergency Service, the volunteers who come for storms, floods and fallen trees.

we_do.title: Brackets or not?
we_do.rule: Decide whether this mention still needs the brackets.
we_do.example:
A) first time you write GPS
B) fifth time you write GPS
items: Thumbs up if it needs the brackets.
Say why in one sentence.
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: A needs the brackets, B does not.
1. SAY: "Okay, same short form twice in the same piece of writing. Only one of them needs unpacking."
2. ASK: "Thumbs up if A needs the brackets." 10 sec, thumbs verdicts, voices off. EXPECT: thumbs up, because the reader has not met GPS yet.
3. ASK: "Thumbs up if B needs the brackets." 10 sec, thumbs verdicts, voices off. EXPECT: thumbs down. Then cold call one student to finish the stem, it needs no brackets because...
4. SCAN every thumb. 80%+ -> move on. Less -> read both mentions in order aloud, then re-ask.
TRAP: thinking every mention needs brackets. Fix: say the reader only needs telling once, student says which mention does the telling.
CLARIFY: if a student asks what happens in a brand new piece of writing, say the count starts again - a new reader has met nothing.
---
Purpose: guided practice on the decision, not the mechanics. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: the rule is per piece of writing, not per paragraph and not per page.

you_do.title: Fix it for a new reader
you_do.rule: Your turn: rewrite each sentence so a new reader can follow it.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
We rang the SES. ->
We rang the State Emergency Service (SES).
items: A) The CFA came fast.    B) Ana used GPS.
C) Our AFL team won.    D) Sam got a PB.
you_do.footer: Check: could a stranger read your sentence?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A Country Fire Authority (CFA), B Global Positioning System (GPS), C Australian Football League (AFL), D personal best (PB).
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one. The sentence keeps every word it had, and the full name is dropped in front of the brackets."
2. SAY: "Rewrite all four sentences in your OG book so a stranger could read them. Three minutes, on your own."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "we unpacked every one of these earlier in the week - start with the first letter and say what word begins with it." Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> rebuild C together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: dropping the short form once the full name is in. Fix: say the reader still needs the short one for next time, student adds the brackets back.
EXTENSION: Write a short paragraph using two different short forms, unpack each one only on its first mention, then underline the mentions that needed no brackets.
HELP: Give the four full names on a card; students match each one to A, B, C or D before rewriting.
---
Purpose: independent application of the whole week in real sentences. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) The Country Fire Authority (CFA) came fast.
B) Ana used the Global Positioning System (GPS).
C) Our Australian Football League (AFL) team won.
D) Sam got a personal best (PB).
EXTENSION: e.g. the Country Fire Authority (CFA) sent two trucks, and the State Emergency Service (SES) sent one. The CFA stayed all night. The third mention needs no brackets.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - fix it for a new reader
you_do.check_rule: Tick each rewrite with the full name first and the short form in brackets.
check_items: A) the Country Fire Authority (CFA) came fast
B) Ana used the Global Positioning System (GPS)
C) our Australian Football League (AFL) team won
D) Sam got a personal best (PB)
you_do.check_footer: Editing move: unpack it once, then move on.
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A Country Fire Authority (CFA), B Global Positioning System (GPS), C Australian Football League (AFL), D personal best (PB).
1. MODEL: "For A I kept the sentence exactly as it was, then swapped CFA for Country Fire Authority and put CFA in brackets straight after it."
2. SAY: "Now tick each rewrite that puts the full name first and the short form in brackets. Fix any that is the wrong way round."
3. ASK: "Which one of these four is not really a name, and how can you tell?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: personal best, because it takes no capital letters.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> rebuild B together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "Take this straight into your next piece of writing. Unpack every short form the first time, then use the short one and keep going."
TRAP: ticking a rewrite that lost the short form. Fix: say the brackets have to hold something, student writes the short form back in.
---
Purpose: protected reveal that closes the week and hands the move to their own drafting. [You Do | Feedback | Grammar | HITS 5]
